 On Wcd, Jul 15, 2015 at 6:11 PM, Noam Chomsky -Ma                            wrote:
  Mathematicians are lucky. Even more so than logicians, who worry about foundations.

  As for the sciences, the luckiest is physics. If a molecule is too big, or some other system too
  complex, they handed over to the chemists — who do the same with the biologists — who proceed to
  the psychological sciences — and then on to history and literature. And of course depth of
  explanation is necessarily sacrificed along the way as complexity mounts.

There are a few exceptions. Parts of linguistics, for example. It would be good to widen that
  bridgehead, but not easy.
  Valeria hasn't been able to leave yet. Maybe in a couple of days.

  On Wed, Jul 15, 2015 at 2:04 PM, Noam Chomsky                                      wrote:
   Some efforts, but nothing satisfying. One problem is a fundamental difference between math and
   science. When a math problem is posed and solved, it's solved. There's a proof. There are no
   proofs in the empirical world. Just better theories, that could be (and usually are) at least partially
   wrong.
